In this manner, repeatedly; again,

As he exhales, pearl necklaces mounted upon all the branches of a pure white tree stand there, having formed pearl parasols for all the Buddhas; likewise, by means of the rays of the sun, everything that is to be known (*jñeya*) disappears from the practitioner’s mind during its state of intense joy. Thereafter, the basis of the practitioner (*yogācārāśraya*) appears, resembling a lunar disk.
It arises within the inner ocean.

A second time, the mind—grasped by the inhalation and taking the form of a young boy—sinks into the outer ocean. Thus, for one who is exhaling while grasping the mind for the sake of concentration, it is grasped by the exhalation within the outer ocean.
And he sees [the Buddha] submerged within the inner ocean, attached to the bliss of meditative concentration;
and thousands of meteors fall into the inner ocean, yet they do not burn or boil, and likewise in the outer ocean.

Sustained by inhalation, that young boy sinks into the inner ocean; sustained by exhalation, he emerges outside and sees crystal pavilions. There, surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds and adorned with pearls, the Blessed One, endowed with mindfulness, arises and ties a white cloth-band, and pearl necklaces [hang] all around his head.
They emerge with silk scarves and pearl necklaces...
Thus, infinite world-systems are seen filled with gabled pavilions made of crystal,
and within them are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds.
In the very same way, [the yogins], embracing their retinue,
remain absorbed in the experience of liberation;
from that state, vajra-like inhalations and exhalations proceed.
In the contemplation of impermanence, the world is pulverized and shattered.
Then, in the third [stage], they set ablaze the entire world through the contemplation of abandonment.
By those very [fires] blazing, the entire world is being boiled and consumed like a mass of foam;
this is the contemplation of dispassion.
Furthermore, in the contemplation of cessation, he sees the basis of the practitioner of yoga as if drenched with cool water, coming to a state of stillness.

At the time of rising, a palace paved with pearls appears; within it, there is a dwelling likewise paved with pearls. The Blessed One then binds a turban upon his head and speaks thus: "Mindfulness of breathing must be cultivated in this way, and when cultivated in this manner, it becomes perfectly fulfilled."
And the gods, filling the entire sky, release a rain of flowers and jewels; this is the cultivation of present mindfulness of breathing (*pratyutpannānāpānasmṛti-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the future cultivation (*anāgata-bhāvanā*):
he sees a low-lying area strewn with pearls, and above that—
The practitioner of yoga (yogācāra), seated upon them, beholds himself as five vast, radiant, and brilliant *maṇi* jewels situated above the solar disc.

He also sees the fully awakened Noble Maitreya surrounded by many thousands of disciples; among those monks, some are seen having attained great height, while others are seen having attained up to the contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupaśyanā*). By this much, one has practiced for the future.
"In this regard, that which is to be cultivated by him will become his root of merit.

Thus, this mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
together with its preliminary preparations and its specific distinctions, is to be described as accomplished.
Therefore, having heard this, neither the teachers of yoga nor the practitioners of yoga should fall into despondency regarding instruction or cultivation.

Beyond this, for those who practice meditation without rejection, the applications of mindfulness, the aids to penetration, and the fruits of asceticism arise, together with their equipment and ornaments.
Immediately following this, the application of the elements (*dhātuyoga*) taught in the *Yogaśāstra* should be pursued; however, we shall here demonstrate only the preliminary practice (*prayoga*).

In that same manner, for one who has performed the preparatory purification through ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, the mind should be fixed upon the opening of the big toe’s nail. Then, the opening of the nail appears like the mouth of a sea-monster (*makara*), and by means of that, one causes the mind to enter.

He places [the mind] upon the crown of the head, fixing it there;
he then binds the mind above that.
Thereafter, like a leather bag filled with various kinds of impurities, he perceives his own physical basis as completely full of such filth.
Therein, one perceives the four great elements: [the earth element], [the water element], [the fire element], and [the air element];
the space element consists of the cavities of the eye and so forth;
and the consciousness element consists of [visions such as] a monkey, a young child, spots, a cluster of lights, and so forth.

In the same way, within the bases of all sentient beings and those not called "sentient," he [perceives] the entire world... [emerging from] the opening of the nail of one toe. From that single opening of the hair-follicle, streams [of water] go forth, filling the great earth as far as the ocean, and they cease within the opening of the nail of the second big toe. Such are the expansion and cessation of the streams.
In this way, there are streams of persons beginning with hair, as well as their radiation and cessation;
likewise, there are streams of persons consisting of various elements,
as well as their radiation and cessation.

Here, one sees the entire basis, its apertures and channels, as empty—thus [seeing] everything designated as both sentient and non-sentient. Then, one sees it broken apart, covered in dust, and so forth;
thereafter, everything falls into ruin and becomes pulverized.
He sees [the world] from the wind-mandala below up to the Aghaniṣṭha heaven above;
he sees those particles of dust as empty within, because this mental attention is conducive to emptiness.

Furthermore, he sees the six elements in the state of the *kalala*, and therein the venomous serpents with the colors of the elements, and in their midst the conch, which is the sign of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).

And within that, he sees the face of a young child, the sign of the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), bound by the thread of life. He sees it growing in the mother’s womb through the successive stages of the embryo (*arbuda*), the flesh-mass (*peśī*), the solid lump (*ghana*), and the branching limbs; and he sees it being born, passing through childhood, youth, middle age, and old age, until it becomes decrepit, diseased, infirm, dies, and is reduced to dust.

In the same way, for all sentient beings, according to their respective capacities, this very "powdered man" (*cūrṇapuruṣaka*) arises as previously described. Immediately thereafter, gladdening the physical basis (*āśraya*) by means of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one then fixes the mind between the eyebrows. From that, a stream issues forth, pierces the circle of earth (*pṛthivīmaṇḍala*), illuminates the hells and the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and pierces the golden wheel (*kāñcanacakra*) and the circle of water (*āpmaṇḍala*).

Having illuminated and transformed the wind-mandala and the space-element, it enters through the navel and exits through the crown of the head; proceeding uninterruptedly as far as the Aghaniṣṭha gods,
it illuminates them, takes up the essence of the four dhyānas, and re-enters through the crown of the head.
Again, one stream issues forth from the middle of the brows and a second from the navel; these two mingle and remain pervading the earth.
First, [the stream] is severed from the middle of the brows, then from the navel.

Then he sees his own physical basis submerged up to the navel, and he perceives the earth filled with trees, upon whose roots monks are seated practicing the application of the elements (*dhātuprayoga*).
And the elements issuing from the openings between his nails pervade the entire world and then dissolve back into those very same makara mouths.
In this way, he sees the earth filled with persons composed of the six elements.
Sometimes he sees the elements individually, sometimes together;
finally, everything is ceased at the navel.

...through mental attention (*manasikāra*) ... arises from the crown of the head; standing with face upward, a star-like point (*tārakā*), adorned with a lattice-work of light, performs entering and exiting through the opening (*chidra*).
Whether it be a lotus or some other [object], he sees all impure substances and the mandalas of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).

Then, from the center of the brows, a stream of Buddhas composed of various jewels issues forth; they are seen seated upon lotuses, entering into the earth element. From that, a dense mass of streams issues out, and the entire world is seen as a single solid mass.

Then, becoming an intensely red color, it enters the water element; those very Buddhas [appear] from those streams of water, and the world is perceived as if [covered] by them. Then, it enters the fire element.
From them, rays of light of various colors emerge;
[they] then enter the wind-element. From those [rays], clusters of wind of various colors emerge and pierce the basis of the practitioner (*yogācārāśraya*). Like snow-clouds...
As if seeing the entire world [in this way],

he then enters the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*). From it, streams of the color of the element of space emerge and enter the basis of the practitioner (*yogācārāśraya*), for that [basis] has become worn out.

The entire world is made of lapis lazuli; Buddhas are seen with bodies composed of pure, clustered dots, and similar streams arrive, [filling] the entire triple world which is the basis for the practice of yoga.
Having pervaded [the world], they remain. Then he sees the entire triple world and the subtle Buddha-bases quivering like drops of dew.
Again, the Buddhas, having taken up lotuses in a condensed manner, strew lotuses over the basis of the practitioner of yoga.
He sees the world as far as the Aghaniṣṭha heaven filled with lotuses, and the Buddhas seated upon them simultaneously, having entered the six elements.
By the streams issuing from them and by the streams of lotuses, like many showers of rain, his own physical basis is filled.
[and] having experienced the bliss of tranquility (*upaśama-sukha*), at the time of emergence he sees himself seated beneath a jewel-tree covered in jewels;
and that jewel-tree [pervades] the infinite world.
Having pervaded [all], he remains; then, from a jewel-tree, he sees the entire ocean of sentient beings embraced by a rain of jewels.
Then he sees the various elevations and hollows, such as the openings and so forth.
And everywhere the word "element" (dhātu) is heard.

The purification of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
He sees the earth filled with other storehouses produced from [the removal of] [perceptions];

The purification of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) [is as follows]:

... [omitted] ... they arise from what is made of clay. Because of that, one sees the earth quaking; this is the purification of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), [revealing] the various root-locations of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
He sees the forehead, the head, and so forth, decaying; both internal and external things, whether designated as sentient or non-sentient, he sees as they decay,

it pervades the entire earth as far as the Aghaniṣṭha heaven. Then...
It is obstructed at the navel.
From there, a stream of Buddhas possessing the radiance of mines [of jewels] arises;
it pervades the entire earth as far as the Aghaniṣṭha heaven.
Furthermore, right there, the conviction resulting from the examination of the aggregate of sensation ceases.

One perceives one's own physical basis as a mass of water bubbles; likewise for all sentient beings. Then, from the left shoulder, a stream of bubbles issues forth and remains pervading the triple world.
Furthermore, bubbles with the color of water appear within the painful body that is ablaze; [and so on] until, within the pleasant body, the faces of women are seen among the bubbles.
This is the sovereign form of passion (*rāga*). When it blazes forth, [the mind] is extinguished right there in that very same place.
Then, from that, a stream of Buddhas, blue in appearance and covered with bubbles, emerges;
having pervaded the triple world, it remains there.
And right there it ceases.
Through the conviction arising from the examination of the aggregate of perception, a stream of rays issues forth from his right shoulder, vibrating;
it then pervades the entire earth.
Then he sees the earth as if covered with golden sand,
and he ceases right there.
Then a stream of Buddhas with golden radiance issues forth and remains, pervading the triple world.
And right there it ceases.

Then, from that tumor, a stream of men emerges, filled with various hollows and cavities, pervading the triple world; and like the collapsing of hollows and cavities in the leaves of a plantain tree, the manifold realm of conditioned formations [ceases], and it ceases at the navel.
From that very navel, a stream of Buddhas resembling space issues forth;
having pervaded the triple world, it remains there and then ceases right there— this is the resolute conviction regarding the examination of the aggregate of consciousness.
From the various locations where [the mind] proceeds, a stream has emerged like that of rivers, pervading the triple world and remaining there;
contained within it...
...is obstructed at the navel.

Within the flames of fire is the fire-tilaka, the sovereign form of consciousness. Furthermore, there are three kinds of formations (*saṃskāra*): meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable. [The meritorious formations] consist of those associated with the three dhyānas of the meritorious formations, and those that lead to rebirth in the formless realms. The non-meritorious formations lead to rebirth in the miserable destinies. The imperturbable formations lead to rebirth in the form and formless realms. These are the formations. The ripening of these formations is experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives. It is not the case that there is no ripening of formations; for if there were no ripening of formations, the noble Dharma and Vinaya would not be established. Therefore, it is known that there is indeed the ripening of formations. This is called the aggregate of formations. What is the aggregate of consciousness? It is the mind, mentation, and consciousness. What is mind? It is the collection of all minds. What is mentation? It is the collection of all mentations. What is consciousness? It is the collection of all consciousnesses. What is the eye-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the eye and forms. What is the ear-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the ear and sounds. What is the nose-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the nose and odors. What is the tongue-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the tongue and tastes. What is the body-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the body and tangibles. What is the mind-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the mind and mental objects. What is the aggregate of consciousness? It is the collection of all consciousnesses. This is called the aggregate of consciousness. What is the aggregate of phenomena (*dharma*)? It consists of the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formation aggregate, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). What are unconditioned phenomena? They are space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). What is space? It is that which provides room and does not obstruct. What is cessation through deliberation? It is the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava*) through wisdom. What is cessation not through deliberation? It is the cessation of conditioned phenomena due to the lack of causes and conditions. This is called the aggregate of phenomena. These five aggregates are collectively called the "five aggregates. What is the internal aggregate of form? It refers to the form within one's own continuum, such as the head, hair, beard, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, stomach, feces, brain, saliva, mucus, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, and so forth. This is called the internal aggregate of form. What is the external aggregate of form? It refers to the form outside one's own continuum, such as grass, trees, walls, fences, tiles, stones, precious gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, gold, silver, crystal, amber, red pearl, emerald, white jade, and so forth. This is called the external aggregate of form. What is the internal aggregate of feeling? It refers to the feelings within one's own continuum, whether pleasant, painful, or neutral, arising from contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. This is called the internal aggregate of feeling. What is the external aggregate of feeling? It refers to the feelings outside one's own continuum, whether pleasant, painful, or neutral, arising from contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. This is called the external aggregate of feeling. What is the internal aggregate of perception? It refers to the perceptions within one's own continuum, perceiving blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, pleasant, unpleasant, distant, near, and so forth. This is called the internal aggregate of perception. What is the external aggregate of perception? It refers to the perceptions outside one's own continuum, perceiving blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, pleasant, unpleasant, distant, near, and so forth. This is called the external aggregate of perception. What is the internal aggregate of formations? It refers to the formations within one's own continuum, such as volition, contact, attention, resolve, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, greed, anger, delusion, pride, doubt, views, and so forth. This is called the internal aggregate of formations. What is the external aggregate of formations? It refers to the formations outside one's own continuum, such as volition, contact, attention, resolve, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, greed, anger, delusion, pride, doubt, views, and so forth. This is called the external aggregate of formations. What is the internal aggregate of consciousness? It refers to the consciousness within one's own continuum, such as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the internal aggregate of consciousness. What is the external aggregate of consciousness? It refers to the consciousness outside one's own continuum, such as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the external aggregate of consciousness. What is the internal aggregate of phenomena? It refers to the feeling, perception, and formations within one's own continuum, as well as unconditioned phenomena. This is called the internal aggregate of phenomena. What is the external aggregate of phenomena? It refers to the feeling, perception, and formations outside one's own continuum, as well as unconditioned phenomena. This is called the external aggregate of phenomena. These are collectively called the "twelve bases" (*āyatana*). What are the twelve bases? They are the eye-base, form-base, ear-base, sound-base, nose-base, odor-base, tongue-base, taste-base, body-base, tangible-base, mind-base, and mental-object-base. What is the eye-base? It is the pure matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the support for eye-consciousness. What is the form-base? It is the visible matter derived from the four great elements that is the object of eye-consciousness. What is the ear-base? It is the pure matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the support for ear-consciousness. What is the sound-base? It is the audible matter derived from the four great elements that is the object of ear-consciousness. What is the nose-base? It is the pure matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the support for tongue-consciousness. What is the taste-base? It is the gustatory matter derived from the four great elements that is the object of tongue-consciousness. What is the body-base? It is the pure matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the support for body-consciousness. What is the tangible-base? It is the tactile matter derived from the four great elements that is the object of body-consciousness. What is the mind-base? It is the collection of all minds. What is the mental-object-base? As he possesses such an intention of loving-kindness, the door of his heart opens.
From them, streams of milk issued forth;
all sentient beings immersed themselves in them and entered their own physical bases (āśraya) by following those very streams.
Upon that foundation, there are lotuses with stalks of lapis lazuli;

and upon their pericarps are milk-pools. Following the stalks of the lotuses, all sentient beings ascend and are seen submerged in the milk-pools, seated upon lotuses with closed petals. From his head, a lotus emerges, and seated upon it, the Blessed One teaches the Dharma.

Upon hearing that, all sentient beings experience a joy equal to that of blooming lotuses; and within those lotus stalks, endless rows of lotuses come into being. Seated upon them, sentient beings are seen in the form of Brahmās.
In this way, while carrying all sentient beings with all their limbs upon his golden body, which is blue, red, and white in color, he experiences supreme joy.
As he carries these beings through walking, sitting, and all other modes of conduct, supreme joy arises within him.
Furthermore, for one engaged in loving-kindness (*maitrī*), neither poison nor weapons affect the body.
A ground made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), fashioned with a lapis lazuli vajra-throne, arises; in its center, the yogin is born with a vajra-natured support, seated upon that vajra-throne.

Above that, all sentient beings hurl all kinds of weapons, but they fall there transformed into flowers. That very Vajrāsana becomes inaccessible to them, and upon those other Vajrāsanas, Buddhas are seen emerging one after another from the upward manifestation of their *uṣṇīṣas*.
By the radiance of their *uṣṇīṣas*, the entire world appears with the luster of sapphire.
By the light of the *ūrṇā* they are white as the moon; by the light of their bodies they are golden-hued;

and by the light of their eight nails they have the luster of rubies. Each of those Blessed Ones encircles one by one the basis of the practitioner (*yogācārāśraya*) from the crown of the head. [He is] like the peak of an immovable diamond mountain.

He remains [there]. Furthermore, even if all sentient beings were to take up every kind of weapon, fire, poison, and so forth, and lions, tigers, and other beasts were to charge at him, from the crown of that one who possesses a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrāśaya*), a river consisting of milk issues forth like a mass of clouds,
filling the entire sky.
Having filled [the world] like a rampart and encompassing all sentient beings, it remains;
and those beings, having laid aside their agitation and weapons, bow down to that very [light].
Furthermore, this other distinction arises for one whose disposition is loving-kindness: his own physical basis [becomes radiant].
He sees himself surrounded by all the causes of death;

then, Brahmās emerge from his physical basis (āśraya) and gaze upon those causes of death. Thereafter, he sees himself liberated from all causes of death, mounted upon the lunar disk, and resembling the moon in appearance.
In the same way, he perceives the removal of death for all sentient beings by means of the conditions for death;
and those sentient beings, through the rays of the lunar disk, enter upward into the superior body,
which is the body of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

That [earth] has Brahmā as its support, and that has the Buddha as its support; within the support of the Buddha, the support of Brahmā is seen, and so on, until within the support of the yogin, the supports of all sentient beings are seen. Therein, the Blessed One—[having entered] the *samādhi* called "The Radiance of the Essence of All Tathāgatas"—walks back and forth upon the earth. When he places his foot down, [a stream] emerges; when he lifts it, he sprinkles it full of that essence. When he sits cross-legged, a milk-tree emerges from his head, pervading the infinite world-systems.

He stands there. As soon as they are sprinkled by the streams of milk that have issued forth, those beings—having cast aside their agitation and weapons—bow down to him who dwells in loving-kindness (*maitrāvihārin*).
Such is the power of one whose intention is imbued with loving-kindness.
How much less so for the Blessed One, the Buddha?

Furthermore, the infinite and boundless ocean of sentient beings becomes manifest before one whose disposition is loving-kindness (*maitrāśaya*). Being consecrated by empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), he is seen; likewise, he is seen as if being consecrated by essences of gold, blue, yellow, red, and white, resembling [the color] of a *jāmbūnada* [gold]. He is seen...
Sprinkled by streams flowing forth from these [lotuses], sentient beings appear as if they themselves were identical to them.
Then, a golden lotus, having pervaded the ten directions, remains embracing all sentient beings.
And from that, equally...

He perceives the distinction among sentient beings; he proceeds with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare of all sentient beings. This is the immeasurable dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrī-vihāra*). It is immeasurable because its basis (*āśraya*) is immeasurable, because its object (*ālambana*) is immeasurable, because its application (*prayoga*) is immeasurable, and because the production of merit (*puṇya-prasava*) is immeasurable. When for a long time his mind, which has been peaceful and is engaged with the resolute intention to benefit all sentient beings, follows along, then through that concentration (*dhāraṇā*), a blue-colored jewel surrounded by blue sprouts arises in the region of the crown; likewise, from all the apertures [of the body], there arise blue-colored [jewels] surrounded by blue sprouts.
Three jewels arise, from which thousands of streams of various essences corresponding to their respective colors issue forth and fall upon sentient beings.

Sentient beings are seen drinking from them; then, from those jewels belonging to one whose intention of loving-kindness has increased, [the essences] emerge from below. Having received them, sentient beings embrace them against their breasts as if they were only sons, and then, from those jewels belonging to one whose intention of loving-kindness has increased...
Having pervaded the entire world, it remains there.

From that [state], one sees the eight great hells along with their sixteen secondary great retinues, together with the cold hells, as well as animals, hungry ghosts, and humans, all stripped of their [defiled] bases. And upon the upper terraces, he sees [them] smooth...

Among the bases of the practitioner (*yogācārāśraya*), the base of the practitioner is thus condensed; it remains as it was before. then, from the sunken region below the midpoint between the eyebrows, a stream of milk issues forth, pierces the circle of the earth, brings all suffering to rest for sentient beings who have gone to the lower realms, and continues until it pierces the circle of wind; having turned back, it enters the navel.

The dominant form:

from that is born a woman with the color of a rainbow, holding ambrosial nectar as it were in a stainless vessel; she casts it toward the ten directions and endows all sentient beings with supreme happiness.

The applications of yoga, the ornaments of yoga, and the specific qualities have been explained; by means of them, all ill-will is to be eliminated, and these benefits arise:
namely, one sleeps in comfort, wakes up in comfort, and while sleeping, deities protect one.
He does not see an evil dream; neither poison nor weapons affect his body.

He is beloved by gods and humans, and is praised by Brahmā. He attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), and having not yet fully realized the higher [stages], he passes away to reach the very nature of the Brahma-world.

The application of that [meditation] is as follows: seeing a friend who is extremely superior, who has fallen into impurity, wearing soiled garments, wretched, blackened, and overtaken by nakedness, concealment, fear, grief, despondency, discontent, stinginess, envy, and malice, supreme compassion arises for him.

In this same way, having seen a neutral person who is weak, as well as an enemy who is weak, middling, or intense, gradually afflicted by those various physical and mental sufferings, compassion arises; then, for him who is thus pained by compassion,
a black and burning boil appears between his eyebrows.

A woman emerges from his head and bathes his body with streams of milk until the sensation subsides; from that body, an ocean of all sentient beings is flooded by streams of milk. Then he beholds the physical and mental sufferings of all sentient beings as they are being destroyed.

Again, in that same way, with a mind focused on compassion, all sentient beings afflicted by physical and mental diseases appear before him. Having seen them afflicted by four hundred and four physical diseases and eight hundred and eight mental diseases, compassion arises within him.
Its dominant form is as follows:
a woman, golden-hued and clothed in white garments, arises in the heart;
once arisen, she encourages the practitioner.

"O you who act for the benefit of all others, I shall provide you with every favorable assistance. Then, from his heart, the form of the Lord of Compassion emerged; like a mass of clouds, it pervaded the entire sky as far as the Aghaniṣṭhā heaven. It released a rain of all necessary provisions as an antidote to the suffering of the whole body, and [it] completely dispelled the mental diseases... [and] obstructed the earth.
With streams of water endowed with the eight qualities flowing from the fingers of both hands, he washed away the remainder of mental suffering. [She] became pure, and her face shone;
likewise, compassion remained established in her heart.
2. He encourages them, saying, "Lift up this being and bathe him!

He then lifts up those beings and bathes them. Emerging from beneath her, he sees beings being sprinkled by Brahmās who fill the sky, holding water-pots in their hands and pouring forth streams of various colors and essences. 3. He sees the beings being thus drenched.
And he bathes her;
the earth is filled with lotuses for the gods,
and he beholds sentient beings mounted upon them.
And rain falls from the fingers of Brahmā’s hand.

Then those beings become filled with joy, and [the Bodhisattva] thinks to himself, "I have pulled these beings out of the mire of great calamity," and thus he directs an exceedingly intense compassion toward them.
From all his pores, silken streamers resembling the sky emerge and remain enshrouding all sentient beings.
Furthermore, with a mind moved by compassion, the eight great hells, together with their sixteen subsidiary hells and the cold hells, appear before him.
And these are the causes for them: those with spears, swords, and staffs in their hands [suffer] in Saṃjīva; in Kālasūtra, there are the cutting of spies’ threads and saws;
in [the hell of] stones and... machines, iron hammers, elephants, and water-pits;
in Saṃghāta, by means of sharp weapons; and in Raurava, they are seized by... [beings].

In the Tapana and Pratāpana hells, there is the entry into cauldrons for roasting and parching; but in the Avīci hell, there is the rain of fire upon the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*), as well as the unshakable [suffering] from the spokes of chariots and spikes.
Seeing this... [for the sake of removing the causes of these beings, I shall thus conceal whatever causes these beings have for their minds.]

For that very one of immeasurable intention, there is a great foundation from which water endowed with the eight qualities issues forth by the thousands; by this, all afflictions are pacified. Then the Blessed One, seated upon the Vajrāsana, teaches the Dharma with a voice that is courageous, profound, and sublime.

5. Having heard that, those beings, passing away from there, are reborn in a happy state. [He says: "Move aside, worthy sir! Move aside! I shall cause the mountain to fall! But even though he speaks thus, the mountain does not move aside.
Then, a great and pleasant touch and a vast foundation pervade all the great hells; the causes [of suffering] perish,
and being completely liberated from all suffering, they abide in happiness.
Again, that man sprinkles it upon his head; out of compassion for him, he [acts] so that all those beings in the hells are being drenched with streams of flower-nectar.
In this way, he sees animals, hungry ghosts, and humans;
and [he sees] those who are suffering due to the five signs of death and the signs of falling from their state,
and he sees the shadow of his own body.
Furthermore, his mind remains fixed upon a single object of focus within the body; his mind becomes capable of maintaining a single objective support and no longer flickers like a whirling firebrand.

For all objects of the senses indeed [become] ... they seize the signs of the five-fold dust, as if with garments [soiled]. Sweat arises on their bodies, and a foul odor overcomes their limbs. The deity does not find stability on his own seat; he who is intent on exertion, the Blessed One, having ascended the lion-throne, arises and teaches the Dharma, and they become agitated.
Uttering the words, "We have seen," they prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One.
Having done so,
they are reborn among the gods.
In this way, he sees as far as the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
Again, with a mind of compassion, he sees the wheel of the five realms of existence revolving; having seen it, compassion arises within him.
To inspire fearlessness, a mountain of afflictions (*kleśa*)— composed of various colors such as attachment,
aversion, delusion, pride, doubt, and views— approaches.
Yet he remains there, undisturbed.

Then that man, taking that wheel of saṃsāra, enters that mountain of afflictions. There he sees the thorns of entry and the various forms of pride; and having seen them, his compassion increases all the more.

In his hand a vajra arises; with it he [shatters] that mountain of afflictions... [the Blessed Ones], mounted upon lion-thrones, teach the Dharma. And Brahmā, taking a water-pitcher, stands before the Bodhisattva and says: "Victory! Victory!"... [he] triumphs.
And he makes a vow for enlightenment;
then that water, tossed by the wind, sprinkles sentient beings in infinite world-systems.

[He] covered [him] with his head; and the Blessed One bound a turban upon his head and said: "Homage to the future helmsman of the world who will appear in the future age! Then the gods, filling the entire sky, having become [invisible], descended. As he was gradually filled with joy and rapture, they released [celestial flowers].

His physical basis, resplendent with the primary marks and secondary characteristics, shines like the orb of the moon; he disciplines sentient beings, and upon arising from that state, a firm superior intention for enlightenment arises within him. His hope remains steadfast, yet seeing those bound again by the fetters of karma and afflictions, an exceedingly great compassion toward them manifests in him.
It arises;
and for one in whom compassion has been born, a sharp, sky-colored weapon arises in the right hand.
By that [light], he severs the bonds of all sentient beings;
and having pervaded the infinite world with a parasol, he remains embracing all beings.
Then follows the consecration of the color of sapphire, as before.
Having gone downward and upward, [he saw] Brahmā mounted upon his swan-chariot;
then the Blessed One and the noble Maitreya, along with their retinues of bodhisattvas, [appeared] before him.
...gate ... he rejoices.
Brahmā says, "May he take breath... ... [he] says, "... you; this is the state of compassion."
Furthermore, immediately after the flow of the consecrations,
that foundation becomes infinite and boundless.

Then a tree made of jewels emerged, pervading the entire world as it stood there. The roots of the tree were established upon a golden wheel, and beneath the tree, golden vessels filled with milk were seen. Beneath the tree, [there were] sacrificial enclosures where the Bodhisattva, giving everything everywhere and at all times, never grew weary; and a man spoke:
In this place, having fulfilled all the heart’s desires of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva attains perfect awakening and, surrounded by an incalculable host of beings,
enters the realm of nirvana without remainder; then, from his heart, a woman arises, golden-hued and clothed in pure white garments.

Bound with a golden garland and a ribbon, she encourages him, saying, "You too, for your part... Then, having bowed down, she makes a vow for awakening (*bodhi-praṇidhāna*). And when he has emerged from that state, his vow—[the rest of the sentence]—falls upon all sentient beings.

Having seen that, and having generated joy and gladness, they emerge and remain embracing the entire ocean of sentient beings. Gradually, they see Buddhas with retinues of many thousands entering the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*). This is another station of compassion (*karuṇāsthiti*).
Furthermore, for one whose mind is fixed upon the space between the eyebrows with a compassionate disposition, an aperture arises.
There he sees the Blessed One;
he sees the world illuminated by the rays of light issuing from him.
He sees the oceans, the continents, the golden wheels, the cities, the palaces, and the gardens.

6. Brahmā, holding a golden vessel, [pours forth] a river resembling the orb of the moon; it issues forth and fills the body. That very stream flows downward as far as the wind-circle and upward as far as the fourth dhyāna, remaining of that same color. Then, re-entering through the crown of the head, it enters the space between the eyebrows.

The second [light] emerges from the navel and fills the station; the station is seen to be completely filled with the constructed abodes of the Buddhas. Then Brahmā appears, mounted upon a swan-chariot.

On its right side there is a golden lotus, and on the left, one with a blue luster. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the Śuddhāvāsa deities, sits upon the pericarp of the lotus on the right; the Śuddhāvāsa deities sit upon the petals, and on the left side is the noble Maitreya, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas sit upon the petals, while he sits upon the pericarp of the lotus.
Then, as he dwells in compassion and has conceived serene faith, a lotus arises at the base of the Blessed One’s feet.
He bows down at the Blessed One’s feet and says:
"O Blessed One, may I in a future time become a guide for all sentient beings,
a remover of the diseases of all sentient beings, a perfectly awakened Buddha. Then the Blessed One stroked his head with his hand and said, "My son."
"In the future time, you shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), the remover of all diseases of all sentient beings.
Then the gods, filled with joy, pervaded the entire sky and released a rain of flowers and jewels upon those seated above the earth.
And from all the pores of the Buddhas, jewel-trees emerge;

seated upon them are the Perfectly Awakened Ones, adorned with moon-maṇḍalas, extending as far as the Aghaniṣṭha gods. The abode of the practitioner of yoga is filled by rivers resembling moon-maṇḍalas that flow forth from their navels.

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the Śuddhāvāsa deities, and the noble Maitreya, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas, ascended upward as they had come; and he, having conceived faith, scattered jewels and flowers,
and the gods searched for them.
This is another state of compassion (*karuṇāsthiti*). Finally, everything is to be known as ceasing within the navel.
Then, the Buddhas, mounted upon lotuses, are seen having entered into one's own body; this is the emergence from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*).
Thus, his compassion—accompanied by its preparatory practice (*saparikarmā*) and distinguished by its excellence (*saviśeṣā*)—is said to be perfected.

Beyond this, the limbs of compassion are now as follows: not causing harm to others, patience, gentleness, mildness, softness, devotion to the welfare of others, and friendliness. When compassion is embraced by these and practiced again and again, it becomes the bringer of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The Blessed One taught sympathetic joy (muditā) immediately after compassion (karuṇā). Therefore, its efficacy is [to be understood as follows]. Furthermore, for what purpose was sympathetic joy taught immediately after compassion? It is said: it is for the purpose of revealing the antidote to envy and aversion immediately after the antidote to cruelty (vihiṃsā).

Either immediately after the mental application characterized by joy at the suffering of others, for the purpose of revealing the antidote to the lack of joy in the happiness of others; or immediately after the mental application characterized by disenchantment, for the purpose of illuminating the mental application conducive to the aspect of gladness (*prāmodya*).

Immediately after the mental attention consisting of the intention to remove suffering, there is the mental attention consisting of the intention to rejoice in [the beings'] welfare and happiness; for the purpose of indicating this, it is asked: what is the intrinsic nature of sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? To that, it is said:

Regarding "mental joy" (*saumanasya*): it has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but when it is grasped together with its attendants (*sānuparivarta*) and its associated factors (*sasaṃprayoga*),
it belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and has the four aggregates (*catuḥskandha*) as its intrinsic nature.

Those belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature; they are based on the desire realm (kāmadhātu) with respect to their support (āśraya), and have the desire realm as their object (ālambana) with respect to their objective referent; [this is] according to the stages (bhūmi).
In the desire realm and in the first two dhyānas, there is mental joy (saumanasya) existing in both ways.

The practice of that [joy] is as follows: one becomes joyful through the happiness of a superior-superior friend; likewise for a middling or mild friend, and likewise for a neutral person. Similarly, one becomes joyful through the happiness of a superior enemy. Then, for one whose mind is fixed upon sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and who is thus resolving upon sentient beings in these various ways, a lotus pond appears in the heart, strewn with golden sand.
He sees beings seated upon golden lotuses with stalks of beryl, studded with jewels, and adorned with every ornament, filled with joy;
having seen them thus throughout the entire earth, gladness arises in him. This is the aspect of sympathetic rejoicing.

And [he thinks], "May beings indeed rejoice! Then, with a mind focused on the practice of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), the ocean of beings, endowed with various forms of happiness and adorned like universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), appears before him.

Furthermore, from his heart, a golden banner is seen to arise; having emerged from his head, it pervades the entire world and releases a rain of all manner of requisites, and finally, a rain of jewels. By means of that, sentient beings perform acts of service toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Within his heart, a woman of golden radiance arises in great joy; she, as the embodiment of the sovereign form of joy, uplifts him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!"
This is well undertaken!
In this very way, sentient beings are favored with happiness in this world and the next;
seeing even the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations made happy with happiness, joy arises.
And the mode of rejoicing is: "May beings indeed rejoice!
Immediately following that, one perceives beings as being made happy by future happiness.

Then, a body resembling that of Brahmā arises for him. From all his pores, moon-maṇḍalas with a golden luster and inlaid with various jewels emerge; he sees sentient beings of similar complexion mounted upon them, as if enveloped within jeweled gabled palaces.

In the same way, the infinite world [is perceived] in the second dhyāna; likewise, for all, there is a blue-colored realm (*dhātu*), and that arises... (as described) in the *Yogalehrbuch* (YL 154V1). Furthermore, the experience and vision of the second dhyāna should be understood as occurring for those free from passion (*vītarāga*) through the forms of sovereign power (*adhipati*), differentiation (*vibhāga*), and natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). ... (as described) in the *Yogalehrbuch*.
By the power of this very method, for one engaged in mental attention, in one part he sees the world of humans and the gods, and in the second part...

[he sees]... endowed with supreme tranquility and control of the mind, possessing a radiance equal to the moon and sun, surpassing fire, lightning, and... the splendor of the Buddhas excels that of the assembly of Śrāvakas.

[He sees] the perfectly fulfilled continuum and the Dharma-body of the Blessed One; and having seen in detail within the *Buddhānusmṛti-vivaraṇa* [the two sides], these are the gods of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), these are the gods of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); these are the gods of conventional birth, these are the gods of purity;
these are happy through the happiness of worldly prosperity, these are [happy] through reliance [on the Dharma]; these have ascended to magnificent palaces and celestial mansions.

These [are adorned] with costly ornaments; these are adorned with the ornaments of ascetics; these are born of lords... these... these are endowed with the equality of the great elements; these are endowed with the equality of the mind.
Then, from the body of the Blessed One, a stream issued forth...

A rain of jewel-flowers falls from the sky. Upon seeing the Blessed One, those beings run toward him from all sides; having bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, the Blessed One teaches them the Dharma. Those beings enter into the ultimate teaching and the conventional teaching. Seeing those endowed with the qualities of a śrāvaka, joy arises.
And the mode of rejoicing is: "May sentient beings indeed rejoice!

Then follows the consecration: a stream of jewels melts, enters through the crown of the head, fills the physical basis, and brings it joy. From his heart, a stream issues forth and disperses, moving downward and upward with the radiance of jewels.
Having illuminated the world, it gradually fills its established state.
Then, the Blessed Buddhas, infinite and boundless, appear seated upon lion-thrones, surrounded by assemblies of disciples; and by the rains of jewel-flowers issuing from them, the world is strewn.
With his fingers, from those very [places], he beholds Buddhas within peaked-roofed pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*) and sentient beings within jeweled palaces; in both of these, [he sees]...
[the world illuminated] by the rays of the qualities of the Buddhas, the world illuminated by the light of the Buddhas' virtues, [resting] upon the foundation of the Buddhas.
At the end, all that is to be known is ceased at the navel; this is the emergence from meditative absorption.

Immediately after sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) was taught by the Blessed One. [This is] for the purpose of revealing the antidotes to sensual desire and ill-will immediately after the antidotes to envy and aversion.
Immediately after the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the [four] immeasurables...
[This is] for the purpose of illuminating that which follows immediately after the mental application (*manasikāra*) conducive to joy regarding the burden of [the practice], and so forth.

From the very beginning, its preliminary application (*prayoga*) is such that—because one has not yet produced [the perception of equality] toward the side of friends (*mitrapakṣa*), whether weak, middling, or intense, nor toward enemies (*amitra*)... [the text continues].
When his [mind] has become thus even and equanimous, then equanimity is perfected.
Now, what is the intrinsic nature of that equanimity? To this it is said:
That [meditative absorption], however, has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature; it is grasped together with its attendants and its associated mental factors.
It is based on the desire realm as its support (*āśraya*) and takes the desire realm as its object (*ālambana*). In terms of its levels (*bhūmi*), it belongs to seven stages:
the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the four dhyānas, and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). It is based on the desire realm... [and so forth].
When one fixes the mind upon the back [of the image] as described, a door appears.
There, for one who fixes the mind upon the lotus-approacher...
[and so forth]... a door appears right there for one who fixes the mind in front; there, those resembling mountain peaks, bearing the form of a Buddha, appear.
Furthermore, there arises here a woman with the color and touch of fresh butter;
she stands embracing him.
Sentient beings are covered by silken cloths that are infinite and boundless; [the cloths] are... [silken cloths].
...among those beings, [there was] mutual indifference toward one another; [yet there was] the essence of affectionate moisture...
[and] for those who were [thus], by means of those [moistures] emerging from them, [there appeared] the color of fresh butter...

2. ... [He is] endowed with compassion for those afflicted by suffering, and with sympathetic joy through rejoicing in both of these; he is joined with [the perfection of] vigor, and is a renouncer. 3. ... [He gives] that to others in order to destroy the faults associated with their expectations; therefore, [he is] ... 4. ...
[He maintains] equanimity toward sense objects.
Equanimity toward sensation; equanimity toward delighting in the conduct of fools; equanimity toward the factors of existence.
Equanimity regarding the conceptualization of a self;
[and] equanimity toward immeasurable objects when the mind is bound to one or another of the aforementioned alternative stations, there arises [this]... (as previously described).
Because of a lack of respect for those who practice misconduct, there arises aversion... [the mind] becomes weary. He perceives the past and future [lives] of those who practice misconduct;
he perceives beings in this way, whether they are beautiful or ugly.
Those with means and those without means; those who have transcended passion and those who have not; the foolish and those free from passion;
those with afflictions and those without afflictions; those who are unconditioned... [and so forth].

And having entered therein, all sentient beings [are transformed]. Equanimity toward sense objects is of three kinds... [omitted] ...therein arises indifference toward neutral sense objects, and aversion is distanced.
There arises [an image] filled with milk, with a moon-disk in its hand;
it has the appearance of an object that is repulsive.

He sees venomous serpents being driven out. Then, [he sees] forms mixed with oil entering through the gateway of the eye, sounds through the gateway of the ear, and odors through the gateway of the nose.

The five tastes are to be touched through the gateway of the tongue; [the objects] through the gateways of the body; and mental phenomena (*dharmas*) through the gateway of the mind. And those constellations, appearing as the forms of desirable sense-objects, ... 6 ... with rays and sparks, they strike at the desirable sense-objects through the gateway of the eye ...
7 ... through the gateway of the ear ... through the gateway of the nose ... through the gateway of the tongue, [they appear as] razors.

Through the gateway of the body, for those possessing power, rivers [flow]... [and] even from that which has issued forth, by means of rays of light, the sense faculties... having grasped the mass of rays, one forms the sign of mindfulness...
The doors of the sense bases (*āyatana*) become oriented toward [the object], and attachment (*anunaya*) becomes distant.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises toward the objects of these three kinds;
consequently, for him, the [clinging] to the objects...
...of those who are disliked among undesirable [objects], and for both of them... he brings about equanimity toward sense objects.
To destroy the faults associated with that [attachment], a woman then appears before each and every sentient being, holding a mirror of infinite extent.
...they attain equanimity toward sense objects, just as...
And he sees each single being, well-attended, seated cross-legged;
this is equanimity toward objects.
What is equanimity toward feelings?

Furthermore, the dominant form of the three types of sensation arises. As it was stated in the *Vedanāskandhaparīkṣā*: therein, within painful and pleasant sensation, a water-colored bubble arises; and as he perceives this, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established.

When he is oppressed [by pain], hatred (*dveṣa*) arises. Therein, his past succession of births becomes manifest before him, wherein he was oppressed and slain by various sufferings. And the future succession of births also becomes manifest before him.
It occurs as follows:

by seeing the fault in the manifestation of hatred, and having seen [the consequences] regarding venomous snakes and the like, he perceives: "This is a fault that has already been committed, and this is a fault yet to come. Thus, toward painful feeling, equanimity is established and hostility is distanced.
And the fault caused by that is averted: in pleasant feeling, attachment arises in one who is experiencing pleasure.
Therein, he brings before him the succession of past births;
therein, under the influence of relishing pleasant feelings, he has committed misconduct and experienced suffering in the miserable realms.

Furthermore, he perceives that [feeling] which is proceeding momentarily and does not persist for even an instant; and having seen this, equanimity (*upekṣā*) becomes established for him toward pleasant feeling, free from distress. Furthermore, being oriented toward the ocean of sentient beings, he bestows equanimity regarding their sensations.

Then, for the sake of destroying the faults associated with that [state], a great palace with pillars of lapis lazuli appears; therein those beings, having seen the disadvantage of the threefold attachment to feeling, gradually attain equanimity. Consequently, they are seen covered by cloths and gabled chambers of the same color, issuing forth from the lapis lazuli pillars. Within the jeweled palace...
"Equanimity toward feeling" refers to the observation that feelings are seen to be of three kinds when one examines them.
Regarding the indifference toward the passion for childhood activities:
therein, his [mind] becomes directed toward the succession of past births—
those belonging to this life and those belonging to other lives.
And he perceives his conduct:

in this life, he was devoted to sexual intercourse, fighting, and watching [such spectacles]; and in other lives, [he was]... by means of becoming a Vaiśvabhū [demon], due to the power of passion, hatred, and delusion, he gave rise to evil conduct and experienced suffering in the states of woe—thus [his history] is of infinite extent.

One perceives the succession of births cast into the states of woe; from that, the form of the sovereign power of moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*avrāpya*) arises. A woman and a man clothed in pure white garments represent these two: shame feels embarrassment toward the afflictions (*kleśa*), while dread of blame feels embarrassment toward misconduct (*duścarita*). Shame is [the cause] regarding misconduct, and dread of blame is [the cause] regarding the fruit of misconduct.
Upon seeing this, supreme shame arises in him,
and equanimity is established toward his delight in the conduct of a child.

Then, for him, the ocean of beings who engage in the play of childish conduct becomes manifest before him. He applies equanimity toward their delight in childish conduct in order to destroy the faults associated with that [delight].

Thereupon, the Blessed One arises, and by the lights issuing from him, sentient beings are illuminated. [They] attain equanimity, and all sentient beings, being stirred with spiritual urgency, [turn toward] the Blessed One.

They go into his presence and even request ordination; the Blessed One ordains them with the formula "Come, monk. Once ordained, they become free from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*). Huts are constructed at the roots of trees, and those beings remain seated cross-legged in equanimity (*upekṣaka*).
Indifference toward the passion for youthful exploits.
What is equanimity toward the factors of existence?

For one who examines dependent origination, the twelvefold wheel of dependent origination—which belongs to the continuum of conditioned formations, pertains to the three realms, and is bound by karma and afflictions—becomes manifest as it revolves; and upon seeing it, a sense of aversion arises within him.

Then, eight Buddha-images mounted upon lion-thrones arise as the presiding forms of the Noble Eightfold Path. By the rainbows issuing from their mouths, the presiding form of ignorance is struck down and ceases; and the twelve-linked wheel of dependent origination becomes disintegrated, appearing like the sky.

The basis of the practitioner of yoga (*yogācārāśraya*) is pressed down by gabled chambers (*kūṭāgāra*). At that time, his mind becomes such that the ocean of sentient beings—constructed by the wheel of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) and bound by mutual karma and afflictions (*kleśa*)—becomes manifest before him. He applies equanimity toward those factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) in order to destroy the faults associated with them.
Then the Blessed One arises, holding a lunar disc; therein, for each and every sentient being, this very sequence of examination arises one by one.
Then, by the rainbows in the form of vajras issuing from the mouth of the Blessed One, all forms of the lords of ignorance are struck down and cease to exist.
They become wheel-less; the twelve-linked wheels of dependent origination of all sentient beings are likewise suppressed by gabled chambers that resemble the sky.
Thus ends equanimity regarding the factors of existence.
What is equanimity regarding the conceptualization of a self?
Here, for the purpose of conforming to the examination of the six elements, there arises [in him] the image of a butcher holding a weapon.
Having slaughtered the cow,
he examines its hide, divided into six sections.
Then, from the navel of the yogin, a blade emerges.
And the yogin places the six cavities of the body’s foundation, part by part, upon that skin; [he places] the right [side], because the earth element is more stable. 3.
Because of its greater stability.
The left [arm] is the water element because it is weaker;
the right arm is the wind element because it is more stable;
the left is the fire element because... by that very [reason].
And for four reasons, the middle cheek of those lying on their left side is digested more quickly because the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is more porous.

The entire face [is assigned] to the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*), because of its pervasive activity. Then, weapons emerging from the basis of the practitioner (*yogācāra*) likewise establish the entire ocean of sentient beings through the division of the six elements, and that which is called non-sentient through the division of the five elements.
He weighs that element with his two hands one by one;
they weigh out equally, and then he says:
"This is the earth element, this too is the earth element; this is the water element," and so on up to "this is the consciousness element.
This too is devoid of self and what belongs to self;
this too is devoid of self and what belongs to self. Then, those six elements and six cavities burn with the fire of revulsion, while other sentient beings [also]...

2. Only the six-element mandalas designated as both sentient and non-sentient remain; then, he weighs those portions designated as sentient and those designated as non-sentient separately with his two hands.
"This too is the earth element," and so forth, as before.
Then, by means of the six-element mandalas...

He sees the three worlds filled; from the sky, streams of oil fall down, and all the mandalas tremble and are withdrawn. Those [mandalas] which were previously described are seen as they vanish. Then, from those drops, the physical basis (*āśraya*) composed of the six elements is produced. A woman holding a lamp—representing the sovereign form of Prajñā—[sees] that destroyed basis as empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
It reveals that "this is merely the five elements.
And therein, by way of a heap of filth, eighty thousand families of worms are seen.
Likewise, the one hundred and four diseases are filled with the venomous serpents of the great elements.

At every door and at every gate, he perceives the five aggregates as they arise; the forms presiding over them are distinguished within the application of the aggregates. In this way, he illuminates all sentient beings, and thereafter he sees the world—whether designated as sentient or non-sentient—as liberated.

He sees this very [conditioned existence] as consisting of various formations, dependent on causes and conditions, devoid of self and what belongs to a self, wandering through the five destinies like a well-trained actor assuming various distinct costumes;
and having seen it thus, equanimity toward these formations arises in him,
whereupon his body is enveloped by crystal-like clouds.

And after a moment, he sees himself inside a crystal gabled chamber; then, within his heart, there arises the form of the sovereign of equanimity—a woman of pure white complexion, clothed in pure white garments, seated cross-legged and remaining in a state of effortless composure.
Then, for him who remains in that effortless state...

4. Thus there is the agitation of water, the agitation of fire, and the agitation of wind, just as during the cosmic destructions (*saṃvartanī*). Likewise, at the end of one's own birth and destruction... [omission] ... 5. Through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established;
it is not due to the fault of cruelty.

And as he dwells thus as one who maintains equanimity, that ocean of sentient beings comes before him; he bestows upon them the equanimity that consists in the conceptualization of a self, for the sake of destroying the faults arising from that [conceptualization]. And for the purpose of bestowing that [equanimity], the Blessed One, having arisen, [emits] rays of light issuing from his own body...

In them, equanimity remains established in that very way, and they are enveloped by mountain peaks made of crystal. In the same way, he sees sentient beings situated within gabled halls made of crystal. What is immeasurable equanimity? ... [text missing] ... what is immeasurable equanimity? It is that which is free from the perception of form, free from the perception of resistance, and free from the perception of diversity; it is the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of pleasure and free from the perception of pain; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended both pleasure and pain, and who has already abandoned mental ease and distress, and who dwells in purity through the feeling of equanimity. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of self and free from the perception of sentient beings; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of a living being and the perception of a person, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of self and other. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of permanence and free from the perception of impermanence; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of permanence and the perception of impermanence, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of permanence and impermanence. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of existence and free from the perception of non-existence; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of existence and the perception of non-existence, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of existence and non-existence. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of eternity and free from the perception of non-eternity; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of eternity and the perception of non-eternity, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of eternity and non-eternity. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of suffering and free from the perception of happiness; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of suffering and the perception of happiness, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of suffering and happiness. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of impurity and free from the perception of purity; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of impurity and the perception of purity, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of impurity and purity. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of emptiness and free from the perception of non-emptiness; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of emptiness and the perception of non-emptiness, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of emptiness and non-emptiness. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of self and free from the perception of non-self; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of self and the perception of non-self, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of self and non-self. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of signs and free from the perception of signlessness; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of signs and the perception of signlessness, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of signs and signlessness. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of desire and free from the perception of desirelessness; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of desire and the perception of desirelessness, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of desire and desirelessness. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of form and free from the perception of formlessness; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of form and the perception of formlessness, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of form and formlessness. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of cessation and free from the perception of non-cessation; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of cessation and the perception of non-cessation, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of cessation and non-cessation. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of arising and free from the perception of non-arising; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of arising and the perception of non-arising, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of arising and non-arising. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of birth and free from the perception of non-birth; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of birth and the perception of non-birth, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of birth and non-birth. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of death and free from the perception of non-death; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of death and the perception of non-death, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of death and non-death. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the conditioned and free from the perception of the unconditioned; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the conditioned and the perception of the unconditioned, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the conditioned and the unconditioned. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the world and free from the perception of the transcendence of the world; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the world and the perception of the transcendence of the world, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the world and the transcendence of the world. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of nirvana and free from the perception of saṃsāra; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of nirvana and the perception of saṃsāra, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of nirvana and saṃsāra. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the Buddha and free from the perception of the Dharma; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the Buddha and the perception of the Dharma, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the Buddha and the Dharma. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the Dharma and free from the perception of the Saṅgha; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the Dharma and the perception of the Saṅgha, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the Dharma and the Saṅgha. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the Saṅgha and free from the perception of the precepts; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the Saṅgha and the perception of the precepts, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the Saṅgha and the precepts. This is called immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, immeasurable equanimity is that which is free from the perception of the precepts and free from the perception of giving; it is the equanimity of one who dwells having transcended the perception of the precepts and the perception of giving, and who dwells having attained the thought of the equality of the precepts and giving. 2. When the parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One is imminent, like a forest shaking at the impact of a diamond mountain, he who follows the Dharma beholds the Blessed One standing before the city of Nirvāṇa, striking the gong of the Dharma; that sound fills infinite world-systems.
He proclaims "M," signaling the time for the disciples to enter the city of Nirvāṇa.
Then, as far as the retinue of that Blessed One extends, from those [lotuses], a mass of flowers and jewels, infinite and boundless in the ten directions, appears, upon which they are seen mounted.
Then, as they were entering the city of Nirvāṇa, a gatekeeper appeared with the luster of lapis lazuli and said: "Whoever has entered this city shall never emerge again.

Having entered, they were enveloped by what seemed like masses of ethereal clouds; like lamps, they were extinguished, becoming cool and tranquil. Thereafter, within their own bodies, there appeared the forms presided over by the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion.

There are seen ten elephants adorned with sun-discs belonging to the [ten] powers (*bala*), and mounted upon them are ten images of Buddhas of the same color, likewise adorned with sun-discs, who remain pervading their respective spheres of activity with light.
Regarding the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), there are four images of Buddhas seated upon lion-thrones, who remain illuminating each of their own spheres with light.
Regarding the three unique applications of mindfulness (*āveṇika-smṛtyupasthāna*)...
Three men, holding vessels of oil as weapons, appear;

from Mahākaruṇā, who is the color of space, there arises in her heart a woman of golden luster, clothed in blue garments, who fills the world with rains of jewel-flowers. Thereupon, the infinite and boundless qualities of Mahākaruṇā are seen residing in the Blessed One.
The disciples are seen mounted upon the solar disk;
within it, five men are visible.
They appear as the sovereign form of the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the sovereign form of [all] qualities, and the [forms] of the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth.

Then, from the heart of the Blessed One, a jeweled lion appears. By this method, the world with its moving and non-moving beings is shaken, and rays of light issue forth; having performed an investigation of sentient beings, they re-enter that very same place. Furthermore, a woman of pure white complexion is seen in the presence of the Blessed One.
And he said:
"The task is accomplished, the vow is fulfilled, those to be trained have been brought to completion, and Nirvana is attained. Then the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; their nature is to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they are extinguished; their complete stilling is bliss.
Having said this, he entered the city of Nirvana and, remaining in a state shrouded like a mass of clouds as ethereal as space, free from all desire, he passed into peace like an extinguished lamp.

What is the recollection of the Dharma?
Here, the noble disciple recollects the Dharma by way of its characteristics: "The Dharma of the Blessed One is well-expounded."

The Dharma is visible in this life, free from fever, not limited by time, leading onward, inviting one to come and see, and to be personally realized by the wise. Upon this earth bounded by the ocean, he then perceives the semen and blood resulting from the union of mother and father; he perceives the consciousness that takes delight therein, and then perceives it being produced in the successive stages of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and the limbs. He sees [beings] thus afflicted by various diseases, dying, dead, being carried out, lying in the cemetery, in the stages from the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) up to the pulverized state; he sees the entire world in this way.
Then, from his own physical basis, a powdered man arises.

Having suppressed those one hundred and seven vital points (*marman*), [they act].
And they remain; and the flow of death, having entered through the crown of the head and blocked all the channels, remains.

There are just as many venomous snakes, which burn the very same vital spots and tendons; he sees his own body motionless, all sentient beings, and the earth as if falling down, while those tendons are being burned.
